cues.text: Let us now turn to chapter three, principles and rights.
This chapter has two halves.
First, the core principles that govern how personal data should be handled.
Second, the rights individuals hold, followed by two practical topics: cross-border transfers and the data protection officer.
Begin with the principles.
There are seven here, and I want you to treat them as a working checklist for any system that handles personal data.
The first is lawfulness, fairness and transparency.
In practical terms, this means you must be able to explain and justify your processing.
If someone asks why you are using their data, and on what basis, you should have a clear and honest answer.
The second is purpose limitation.
You collect data for specified, legitimate purposes.
If you later want to use that data for something new, you must assess whether the new use is compatible with the original purpose.
And where required, you must also establish an additional legal basis.
So a purpose is not a blank cheque; it sets boundaries.
The third is data minimisation.
You collect what is necessary, rather than everything that is potentially useful.
Notice the contrast.
"Potentially useful" is a tempting standard, because more data often feels better.
The principle says the test is necessity.
The fourth is accuracy.
Data that is outdated or erroneous must be corrected.
A record that was right five years ago may be wrong today, and decisions made on wrong data can harm the person concerned.
The fifth is storage limitation.
You retain data only as long as it is justified.
That means you should define deletion and archival rules in advance, rather than keeping everything indefinitely.
The sixth is integrity and confidentiality.
This requires appropriate technical and organisational security.
Technical measures might be things like access controls; organisational measures are things like policies and training.
The source asks for both kinds.
The seventh is accountability.
It is not enough to follow the principles; you must be able to demonstrate that you do.
You do this through records, governance and review.
Now to rights.
Individuals may have rights of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection and portability.
They may also have the right to withdraw consent, and safeguards around automated decisions.
But note the qualification: all of this is subject to each law's scope and exceptions.
Rights are not identical everywhere.
Several distinctions matter here.
First, portability is not simply deletion.
Portability enables an individual to obtain, or transfer, qualifying data in an appropriate format.
It is about moving data, not removing it.
Second, erasure is not absolute.
Legal retention obligations may justify keeping records even when someone asks for deletion.
Under the GDPR, the right to erasure comes with statutory exceptions, found in Article 17.
Third, compare the GDPR with HIPAA.
HIPAA provides rights such as access, and requests for amendment.
It does not provide a general deletion right equivalent to the GDPR's.
So you should never assume that a right in one law exists in another.
Next, cross-border transfers.
Transferring personal data across borders requires a relevant legal basis or safeguard under the applicable rules.
Under the GDPR, examples include adequacy, or appropriate contractual safeguards.
When evaluating a transfer, you should consider the destination country's law, the risks of access to the data, onward transfers, and processor arrangements.
Two cautions follow.
Neither the location of a cloud region nor encryption alone proves compliance.
Where the servers sit, or whether the data is encrypted, does not by itself settle the legal question.
And in the Nigerian context, the NDPA does not impose a blanket requirement that every record be stored in Nigeria.
So you should not assume data localisation is required for everything.
Finally, the DPO, the data protection officer.
The DPO advises, monitors and supports compliance, and also supports liaison with the regulator, with appropriate independence.
Independence matters, because a DPO who is pressured to approve everything cannot monitor effectively.
You must determine the applicable appointment and registration obligations.
That includes the position of Nigerian controllers and processors of major importance.
Do not assume every entity has identical duties.
And one last, crucial point: a DPO is not a substitute for controller accountability.
The organisation that controls the data remains responsible, and appointing a DPO does not transfer that responsibility away.
